Experience, Interpretation, Self-Knowledge:—The Lost Uniqueness of Kohut's Self Psychology

Benjamin Wolstein Ph.D.

Benjamin Wolstein

Benjamin Wolstein, Ph.D.
2 West 67 Street
New York, New York 10023

Benjamin Wolstein  

H. Kohut, How Does Psychoanalysis Cure? Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984.

KOHUT'S VIEWS OF PSYCHOANALYSIS set forth in this, his final, volume hold no surprises for those readers who have followed the statements of his evolving ideas in his two previous major efforts, The Analysis of the Self (1971) and The Restoration of the Self (1977). Most important of all is the centrality he continues to confer on the outer social and interpersonal side of the self, what he terms the "selfobject, " as both real and internalized, and the practical deemphasis on the inner psychic and individual side, the "selfsubject" in his term, as both imagined and externalized. Difficult though this may be to comprehend about his newly announced, self-described innovation in contemporary psychoanalysis, it is, nonetheless, still true that the psychic self as a dynamic point of origin, or source of its own uniqueness, still fails to receive the attention it deserves in his work. Or for that matter in general psychoanalytic inquiry. So his version of self-psychology proves, in the end, to be insupportably one-sided: it provides for no more than a truncated psychology of the self, lacking as it does a point of dialectical tension for psychic movement toward both connectedness and separateness from within.

Robert Langs  

THE ISSUE OF THE SCIENTIFIC STATUS of psychoanalysis is of concern to us all. For the clinician, it is essential that psychoanalysis offer a foundation that meets accepted scientific standards. For his or her patients, the assurance of a scientific foundation to psychoanalysis promises the best possible cure available at the moment. And for the clinical researcher, there is a need to develop research approaches founded on a philosophy of science that promotes suitable forms of measurement, prediction, and perhaps above all, opportunity for new discoveries and advancement.

It is the main thesis of the present paper that psychoanalysis is in principle and in large measure—though of course, not entirely—an Aristotelian science.1 As such, it is primarily naturalistic, based on common sense observation and the statistical norm, concerned with the "essential nature" of the psyche's presumed elements, and intent on classifying those elements in terms of their apparent attributes and predetermined course of development. It is my intention to present arguments designed to reveal the Aristotelian spirit and philosophy at the heart of psychotherapeutic and psychoanalytic endeavor in both theory and practice.

LANGS' MAJOR CLINICAL CONTRIBUTIONS have been in the area of appreciating the latent content of patients' productions by deciphering encoded material. He has shown that the instigation of derivative material invariably involves the therapist's interventions. The validity of his interpretations is demonstrated by the derivative confirmation or disconfirmation contained in the material following interpretation. The scientific method expects that theories predict results. And, indeed, skeptical, open-minded practitioners have been able to duplicate Langs' results. His interests have led him to investigate the nature of unconscious priorities: his seven-fold dimensions of unconscious mentation were determined by analyzing the various preoccupations of derivative communication. And now he has described a new model of the mind to help understand the dual nature of mental functioning (Langs, 1986a), (1986b).

Langs has formulated a topographic model that explains the voluminous clinical data he and colleagues have collected over the past seven years.

The three papers (followed by Langs' reply) are responses to Robert Langs' "Clinical Issues Arising from a New Model of the Mind", which appeared in this Journal in July 1986, 22:418–444.

LANGS' (1986A), (1986B) NEW MODEL OF THE MIND fills an urgent need for models and theories which are consistent with clinical observations and congruent with contemporary knowledge of information processing in the brain. Today there is a special need for information processing models which take into account what Langs calls "emotionally charged messages and information" (p. 1). Gardner's (1985) book, The Mind's New Science, describes the neglect of affectivity by cognitive scientists in the disciplines of psychology, linguistics, anthropology, and the neurosciences. Gardner writes:

"Though mainstream cognitive scientists do not necessarily bear any animus against the affective realm, against the context that surrounds any action or thought, or against historical or cultural analyses, in practice they attempt to factor out these elements to the maximum extent possible." (p. 41, italics mine.)

Psychoanalysis can make a unique contribution to understanding human behavior by its discoveries about the role of affect in cognition and action.

Support for Langs' model comes from many investigations in the fields of cognitive psychology and neuropsychology. Langs' concepts of a synthesizing center and a message analyzing center which operate outside of awareness and give meaning to incoming stimuli is supported by numerous experimental studies. Cognitive psychologists demonstrate that individuals unconsciously and, for the most part automatically, monitor, evaluate and respond to incoming stimuli. The brain unconsciously performs a constant "meaning analysis" in which the world is being interpreted and appropriate schemas are automatically activated (Mandler, 1984). Though high-level meaning analysis includes conscious evaluations, lower levels of meaning analyses proceed automatically and unconsciously.

Langs' model emphasizes the "intelligence" of the Deep Unconscious System.

WHEN I WAS AN INTERN AT A Veterans Administration Hospital twenty-four years ago, my first psychotherapy patient was a chronic schizophrenic male who I saw three times weekly for a year. He was my contemporary, from an upper middle class assimilated Jewish family, a graduate of an Ivy League School, who had become psychotically ill while in basic training. He had been residing at this hospital for several years. An attractive, crew-cut man, muscularly built, with piercing blue eyes that were at the same time glazed and blank, he wore cigarettes in his ears.

During the next months, he became engaged as did I, the cigarettes came out of his ears, his eyes became alive and his communications though indirect became more comprehensible. One particularly gray day, pretending to read the "Times" and not looking at me, he was smiling broadly and commented "The sky seems very blue today." He had been coming regularly to sessions and it was obvious that he was very happy. At another meeting, he told me that he was thinking of getting a puppy. I understood that he wanted to care for the child part of him that he had neglected and that had been abandoned by his cold, distant mother and unavailable achievement-oriented father. He began to go out on passes and to speak more directly about his adolescent and college years where he had felt so alone and alienated. There was a mutual excitement and appreciation of the connection we had made.

I periodically tried to remind us both that I would be leaving in a year. Still, I was not fully prepared for his reaction when I finally said I would be leaving at the end of the month. He said nothing, but his eyes went blank and he simply left the room. I went to his ward: The cigarettes were back in his ears and he looked through me as though I weren't there. I returned a few more times but he acted as though I did not exist. I dreamed that I was following him down corridors never being able to catch up with him.

Nature and Utilization of Transference Phenomena (Panel Presentation)—Introduction

Gloria Friedman Ph.D.

Gloria Friedman

Gloria Friedman  

THE CONCEPT OF TRANSFERENCE WAS originally used to describe and understand a cluster of reactions by the patient that occurred during the course of an analysis. While that simple view is still largely accepted, there is a wide diversity of opinions as to why transference occurs, what it means, how it is to be utilized by the analyst, and what its significance to successful treatment is.

All three authors on this panel agree that the concept of transference designates behavior and feelings on the part of the patient that occur in treatment. Where they differ from the classical position is in their belief that transference develops out of a particular patient-therapist relationship. Steeped in the interpersonal tradition, the authors are acutely sensitive to the effects not only of the personality variables involved, but also of the impact of the analyst's theory, technique and even language on the very existence of a particular transference reaction. This is a far cry from viewing transference as a simple unfolding of a patient's pathology.

Thus it is entirely possible, in fact probable, that certain aspects of a patient's personality will not become a focus for analysis in a given patient-therapist dyad because it is inattended to by the analyst, or because it does not develop in the particular interpersonal field that evolves between the patient and his or her analyst. Each author addresses this issue focusing on different aspects of the problem.

This panel was presented at the Scientific Symposium "Clinical Controversies and The Interpersonal Tradition" on November 15, 1986 in New York City, under the auspices of The William Alanson White Institute.

TO BE INVITED TO GIVE A Glover Lecture for a second time is an honour which is difficult to decline. It also seemed an impossible challenge considering Edward Glover's2 contributions to the study of sexual deviations covering a period of 40 years. After some hesitation, I found the stimulus for this presentation in something Glover said in his paper on "Aggression and Sadomasochism" which he gave at a symposium organised by the Portman Clinic in 1963: "it will be maintained that one of the important functions of sexual perversions is defensive in nature, a kind of organised sexual adaptation which, however, may in many instances bring a variety of ego-disorders in its train." He added: "the pervert protects his reality sense from gross interference." (Glover, 1964).

Those words had been in mind for a great many years but now with my own added experience, I asked myself the question: Is that the reason why perverts are so difficult to treat? In the case of a fetishist, for instance, the psychic reality which he protects is that there are no sexual differences, a wholly illusory belief, shared by the man or woman who dresses or acts as a person of the opposite sex. Is it possible that by protecting their distorted reality sense perverts succeed in protecting some hard core of ego disturbance, which threatens the whole of their being? It seemed that perhaps this could be a better line of understanding the therapeutic challenge we constantly face in this field, rather than the popular misconception that a perversion is not given up because it is pleasurable. On the contrary, we know the misery of the perverts' lives as they go in search of their ephermeral satisfactions.

IDENTIFICATION OF AN "AMERICAN SCHOOL" marks a shift both in the geographical and in the theoretical orientation of psychoanalysis (Wolstein, 1977), (1985). The convergence of European and American thought in the United States between the late 1920's and the 1950's enriched psychoanalysis with sociocultural and ego-interpersonal considerations unexplored in classical psychoanalytic inquiry (Fromm-Reichmann, 1959) ; (Held-Weiss, 1985); (Thompson, 1984). Today, shared sociocultural orientations may unite American clinicians more closely than metapsychological positions differentiate among them (Levenson, 1972).

The American School merits consideration apart from geography and sociology. The term underscores a pluralistic orientation grounded in American psychological soil, both receptive to European psychoanalytic thought and nurturant of continued growth in the American grain.

The first systematic formulation of American psychology dates to 1890, with William James's publication of The Principles of Psychology. James's psychology of consciousness synthesizes observational and experiential processes both as the subject and structure of psychological inquiry. The dialectic of Jamesian psychology encompasses consciousness both as a unitary phenomenon and as reflexive attention to specific aspects of the whole phenomenon.

WHILE ENTITLEMENT IS USUALLY DISCUSSED in terms of narcissistic and borderline patients, I believe disorders of entitlement are a matter of degree and cut across diagnostic categories. In grandiosity, there is an overabundance of entitlement and overt anger that frequently masks an intolerable feeling of shame, a fear of being exposed as vulnerable and needy. In subservience, a paucity of entitlement often masks self righteous rage and envy. In grandiosity there is self-idealization at the expense of others who are depreciated. In subservience there is idealization of others and denigration of oneself. I shall be focusing on grandiosity.

Disorders of entitlement—particularly when they are adhered to rigidly—can, and usually do, provoke strong countertransference reactions in the analyst. How she uses the countertransference depends on her personal style and theoretical orientation. Her theoretical orientation may in turn to some extent justify her personal style.

My own leaning is toward trying to help both patient and analyst expand their possible choices.

Dale Ortmeyer gives an overview of the psychoanalytic thinking concerning aspects of idealization, especially in terms of transference, and includes Sullivan's often overlooked statements concerning the developmental function of pre- and adolescent idealization of peers and of projections of the person-to-be.

IHAVE BEEN IN THIS BUSINESS about half as long as Dr. Witenberg and it's nice to have many of the observations that I have made during this short period of time confirmed by his much wider and longer experience. I think what I'll do first is summarize the many areas of agreement and then focus on several areas in which I might change the emphasis a bit in his presentation.

The major theme that I loved in Dr. Witenbergs' talk could be paraphrased as something like, "everyone should read about theory with an awareness that they're doing it at their own risk and also at the risk of the patient." There should be some precautionary label on every book by a psychoanalytic theoritician. There's nothing that ruins a good therapist more than becoming overly devoted to an archaic non-commonsense theory. And no theory ever tells us what to do in the room at a particular moment, nor should it in any specific way. There are many people whom I thought were excellent therapists when I trained them as residents to whom I can't refer patients now, when I realized that the therapists changed a lot. They've learned more along the way and I don't want my patients subjected to what they've learned. That's not to say that there's no place for theory. It does provide a very useful framework. It can be a transitional object as Dr. Witenberg mentioned—it's a comforter, it can provide a rationale for what we do; or magic; or a metaphor. Theory guides the overall practice but shouldn't intrude too much on the therapists' intuition in the room. I think that doing therapy is a little bit like hitting a fast ball. A good deal of what goes into hitting a fast ball or throwing a fast ball one is born with. The skill could be trained somewhat and improved but it can also be worsened if there's too much attention to detail without focussing on the current needs of the situation. We don't want to make great natural hitters too self conscious.

Another point that Dr. Witenberg makes that I think should be made more explicit is that most of the great theoriticians have been fairly naive epistomologically and, fairly naive scientifically.

DR. STERN ADDRESSES A NUMBER of problems in his discussion of how transference becomes knowable. While he never really provides us with his definition of transference and how, for example, it differs from other unformulated experiences, he does lay the groundwork for how therapist and patient work together. He is primarily concerned with the process by which transference becomes known to the patient and analyst, and argues for the centrality of words in defining and in turn influencing the transference experience. In effect, certain reactions of the patient are addressed and designated as transference by the analyst, and until such formulations are made, they are not experienced or known as transference and hence not explored and analyzed.

In describing this process, Dr. Stern examines the process of thinking and what the necessary mental attributes are for such learning to take place. He does not see transference as a fixed phenomena "in" the patient, but as reactions by the patient that are organized by the analyst's words. He stresses that this is a process of selection, and like others before him, points out that this is where the particular analyst and patient interaction becomes significant in how one and not another transference formulation is chosen. It is the possibility of alternative meanings that ultimately helps to dislodge the patient's imbeddedness and thus expand the patient's awareness.

IT WAS WITH GREAT INTEREST that I read Dan Stern's book. In it he brings together his voluminous and multifaceted direct observations of infants and their mothers with developmental and psychoanalytic theories. My interest had to do in part with learning more about infants, especially their unfolding relationships with their mothers, based on observed behavior rather than retrospective speculation. It also had to do with the possible ramifications of Stern's work for a revitalization of psychoanalytic theory and practice. I was not disappointed.

Inevitably we, as adults, project onto others—including infants—what we experience ourselves. However, it is one thing to hypothesize about infancy retroactively with apparent corroboration from a select group of troubled and impressionable adults seen in analysts' offices.

WHILE FREUD RELUCTANTLY ABANDONED the Project for a Scientific Psychology, his attempt to formulate a neural basis for psychic functioning, later psychoanalysts have been more content to work in a purely psychologic realm. The mainstream of thought in psychoanalysis has been shaped by clinical experience, with little appeal made to neurophysiological criteria in judging theoretical developments. The growth of sleep research following the discovery of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep, activity which directly addressed a function of central concern to psychoanalysis, has managed to provide only a catwalk between the two disciplines. Data gathered in the laboratory concerning dream content has in fact been cited by opponents of psychoanalysis in order to discredit its theories.

Against this background of mild hostility and greater indifference, the quixotic Jonathan Winson, an accomplished neuroscientist at Rockefeller University, began to formulate in the late 1970's a theory regarding the neurologic substrates of the unconscious, drawing upon both an extensive background in neurophysiology and a respectful reading of Freud. Presenting this theory in Brain and Psyche: The Biology of the Unconscious(1985) Winson proclaims: "The key to understanding the brain mechanisms underlying the psyche lies in elucidating the means by which the hippocampus, limbic system, and prefrontal cortex process information and build a behavioral strategy. The research path has in part been traveled" (p. 241).

Introduction

HARRY STACK SULLIVAN HAS MADE A significant contribution to child and adolescent psychiatry. A typical paradigm is the children's mental health centre Redbank House, at Westmead Hospital, in Sydney, N.S.W. This centre includes a community outreach programme, outpatient, day-patient and in-patient services. For the younger children, in-patient admission consists of whole family admission and a consistent application of family systems plus milieu therapy. For the adolescent in-patient and day-patient programme, a systems approach is utilized with the peer group sub-system involved in group psychotherapy, patient-staff therapeutic community meetings, team-family therapy and individual psychotherapy for selected patients. An ecological systems point of view (Auerswald, 1972) is used as an envelope into which is integrated systemic family therapy theory and Sullivanian interpersonal theory (Siegel, 1986).

In this paper, I will elaborate on the Sullivanian interpersonal theory component of the larger systems envelope and will try to demonstrate how that model was the logical precursor of family and eco-systemic theory. I will also endeavour a critical re-appraisal of Sullivan's work in the light of developing object-relations and self-psychology theories.

Harry Stack Sullivan created a major revision of psychoanalytic theory.

EDITORS OF INTERNATIONAL PSYCHOANALYTIC journals which are, in effect, ambassadors of training institutes and/or analytic societies, face problems of manuscript selection and production that are homologously, remarkably similar to those conflicts being confronted by colleagues elsewhere. That is, many of us in various functions in our profession, struggle constantly with issues relevant to admissions to training institutes, standards of excellence, courses, appointments to faculty, awards of merit, and ultimately anything pertaining to acceptability. Our choices and actions are especially painful, when we come to believe that clinging to hopefulness forces us to dilute our standards. It is probably the same in our society at large particularly in other professions and especially in academe. It seems evident that choices must be informed in such a way that whatever we do does not make us rage against ourselves, or despair against our disappointment and natural, creeping cynicism.

The end product must reflect positively on itself, obviously, its sponsoring institution, its authors, and our profession. I will not discuss here the necessity that editors give some thought to aesthetics, which would include the size of their journals, their typographical design and the quality of the paper used.

IT IS A PLEASURE TO DISCUSS Dr. Basch's paper. The paper, in the spirit of his previous writings, speaks with both force and moderation of the potential of Kohut's self psychology to operate as a unifying theoretical framework. Within this framework, Basch believes, apparently disparate psychoanalytic models not only can coexist peacefully, but can even complement each other in illuminating the recesses of personality development and psychopathology.

Basch claims that Freud made one monumental discovery: the existence and power of unconscious motivation. This is the only aspect of his theory capable of confirmation by clinical observation, and it is one which continues to stand up to contemporary neurological research. Along with this discovery, unfortunately, came an equally monumental mistake: Freud's dual instinct theory, with its special emphasis on the central motivational role of psychosexuality. Never even a genuine psychological theory to begin with, the dual instinct theory is discredited by biologists, although it continues to attract Freudians like moths to a flame.

So, Basch argues, the future of psychoanalysis rests on our ability to detach ourselves from our fatal fascination with drive theory.

I WANT TO PRESENT MY OBSERVATIONS on the relationship between theory and practice as the result of having been in the field for 39 years and six months. The context within which I present this, of course, is as a member of an Institute which has had, and continues to have, an open-ended approach to both theory and practice. The assumption is that the final answer is not in; we do not have the final theory or the final way to practice. We know that we help people who come to us. We are only on the verge of knowing how this help works.

As a result of the open-ended approach I think I have come to understand almost all theories. My position is: I love all theories but I fall in love with none of them. When I study theories, I feel enlightened and get clearer about my premises. I find a theory particularly helpful when I can say, "Yes, of course. That's true. I have never put it into words before." A USEFUL MODEL IS AN EVOLVING design rather than a fixed configuration. Created to explain and clarify previously disparate observations and to help resolved vexing clinical and theoretical issues, discussion and research into the model are bound to bring refinements.

A good model should create new concepts, ideas, and challenges. It should serve to evoke debate and to generate additional fresh ideas. Such a model should raise as many questions as it resolves. And eventually, with extended investigation and reconsideration, the model should give way to a new creation which resolves the newly discovered flaws in the initial presentation.

The three excellent and probing papers by Dorpat, Goodheart and Simon seem to attest to the viability of the new model of the mind to which they are responding (Langs, 1986, In press). In the present paper, I will offer further clarification and addenda to the model, ideas that have emerged through my clinical and supervisory experiences subsequent to its inception. Secondly, I will discuss the hypothesis that there are two distinctive modes of repression as a way of illustrating the necessity for, and the distinctions between, the two basic systems of the mind I have postulated—the conscious system (with its own superficial unconscious component) and the deep unconscious system. Thirdly, I will respond selectively to the three discussants and attempt to resolve some of their cogent challenges to and questions about the model I have proposed. Finally, I will discuss briefly the necessity to research this model of the mind and the importance of doing so by introducing a new branch of scientific endeavor—the development of mathematical models and other mathematical approaches to mental phenomena, including the therapeutic interaction and basic models of mental functioning.

IT IS CURIOUS THAT THE word "entitlement" has been incorporated into the psychoanalyst's vocabulary. Its usage is more common in the fields of sociology, political science, and law. The Oxford English Dictionary defines entitlement: "to furnish a person with a title to an estate. Hence generally to give a person a rightful claim to a possession, privilege, designation, mode of treatment, etc." It may be that our current society, so obsessed with materialism and litigiousness, has influenced the incorporation of this word into our clinical language.

In considering entitlement psychologically, it is useful to examine the unconscious experience that may be masked. As Groddeck was so fond of demonstrating, conscious attitudes often belie their unconscious roots, through negation. Where there is conscious hate, there is often unconscious love. Where there is conscious tenderness, there can be unconscious rage. If we are to extend this sort of psychology to entitlement, we shall have to decide: what is the inverse of entitlement?

I BEGAN MY PSYCHIATRIC TRAINING in 1954. One of the first weekly staff conferences given by the chief of my department dealt with the sexual nature of infant behavior and its subsequent effects on character formation. During the question period, I innocently asked how we knew, since infants could not speak to us, that their behavior was indeed sexual. I was not prepared for the tirade that followed, nor do I remember all that was said, but I do vividly recall that it was frequently punctuated by the suggestion that if I could not accept the truth of the basic principles of psychoanalytic theory I knew where the door was, and was free to use it. In this way I was rather rudely introduced to the idea that perhaps all was not well in the field in which I had chosen to spend my professional life.

As you can see, I did not take the implied suggestion that perhaps surgery or internal medicine might benefit more from my

The controversies that led to the foundation of the White Institute concerned a number of issues, many of which were addressed during this symposium. The founders of the Institute insisted that there could be no valid psychoanalytic theory that did not give due prominence to the importance both of the cultural and of the relational or interpersonal factors either in conceptions of the development of the individual or in the vicissitudes encountered in the psychotherapeutic encounter. Parallel concerns were reflected in the English school in the works of Fairbairn, Winnicott and Guntrip. A similar interest was later developed in this country with Kohut's concern about the development of the self in relation to significant others, both in psychological development and in therapy. The theories of the ego-psychologists may be seen as a half way mark in the conceptual evolution from a determinist libido theory position to an interpersonal perspective on human development.

Clara Thompson, a founder of the White Institute, along with her colleague, Karen Horney, wrote pioneering articles which threw new, and now widely accepted, light on the cultural and interpersonal factors instrumental in the development of feminine psychology. These views were not favorably regarded at the time. Harry Stack Sullivan, Frieda Fromm-Reichmann, and Erich Fromm, also founders of the White Institute made towering contributions to the cultural and interpersonal aspects of human development that were controversial in the early days, but are now basic to our understanding of the human condition.—From the Welcoming Address by John L. DURING THE LAST TWO DECADES, the psychology of the self has been moving to the center of psychoanalytic attention. And it promises to remain a dominant factor in therapeutic inquiry for a number of reasons. Consider but a few, especially as background for the present discussion. First, empirical: After the failure of a consistently instinctual-libidinal approach to interpretive metapsychology, and as the patient's ego or self-system increasingly became part of direct psychoanalytic inquiry since the 1930s, a patient could perceive aspects of a psychoanalyst's personality even beyond the psychoanalyst's own self-awareness. Second, systematic: After the cracking of the metaphor of the uninvolved mirror, and as countertransference, counterresistance, and counteranxiety increasingly became part of direct psychoanalytic inquiry since the 1950s, psychoanalysts could each use their psychic resources in their own individual ways directly in their therapeutic work with patients. Psychoanalytic Interpretation in Modern, Clinical Perspective—"A Flight from History"11

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski, M.D.
250 East 87th Street
New York, New York 10128

Gerard Chrzanowski  

THE PURPOSE OF THIS PAPER is to offer an updated, clinical version of interpretation in psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic practice. The art of interpretation is now considered part of a distinctly dynamic process within an intersystemic, or interpersonal frame of reference. A change has taken place in the way primary, clinical data are obtained and incorporated in the therapeutic process. In particular the great complexity of the relationship between past and present has emerged as an intricate field of investigation which has largely replaced the emphasis on cause and effect. In a similar vein the relation between fact and fiction, truth and figure of truth has assumed a different significance. Earlier criteria for pursuing the truth based on the principles of the natural sciences have become problematic when applied to the human condition. In its place the intermingling of fictive, subjective or experiential components with factual data in the analytic process has taken on a more prominent position in the complex process of interpretation.

Viewed from a one dimensional position, interpretation is a rather presumptuous term, as Karl Menninger pointed out many years ago. The term tends to imply a measure of factuality and authenticity while minimizing its basic subjective quality.

PULLING AT A LOOSE THREAD INADVERTENTLY may unravel an entire seam. In much the same way, focusing on the clinical symptom of entitlement initially seemed a modest enough enterprise. Gradually, however, it emerged as so prevalent and significant that, as one journal article has suggested, it, "may be a major factor in psychopathology." (Kreigman, 1983) Such a judgment seems excessive, at least if one goes by the meagre half dozen articles focused on this topic in the psychodynamic literature. Equally, it is excessive if one considers that entitlement is noted only once in DSM III (p. 317), and then merely as one of several traits which in combination constitute a single criterion among five pointing to a particular diagnosis, albeit a currently fashionable one, that is, Nacissistic Personality Disorder.

Perhaps concentration on any one symptom tempts the clinician to magnify its importance, given the nature of psychodynamic conceptualization in which everything connects with everything else, and not always very precisely. Thus entitlement is linked with self-image, idealization, grandiosity, need gratification and the reality principle, not to mention social role, exploitativeness and so forth. In fact, thinking about such ramifications makes it clear that, DSM III notwithstanding, attitudes about entitlement are relevant to more than narcissistic personality disorders.

Unformulated Experience and Transference

Donnel Stern Ph.D.

Donnel Stern

Donnel B. Stern, Ph.D.
8 West 65th Street

Donnel Stern  

TRANSFERENCE DOES NOT ATTAIN a form compatible with words until that moment in the treatment in which it is described. In fact, the words used to describe transference give it its shape and meaning. Prior to its description transference is not explicitly meaningful. Unformulated transference exists in a vague and indeterminate state which, if it were worded, could be spoken in more than one way, perhaps several ways. And since the description eventually chosen is jointly chosen by patient and analyst, the very shape and character of the patient's transference experience, its warp and woof and not just its meaning, is a product not only of the patient, but also of the analyst, and of the interaction between the two. These points have been approached from several directions in the psychoanalytic literature, especially from the interpersonal perspective. I will approach them through a discussion of language.

Transference is a description of certain aspects of the relationship between patient and analyst, and like any description it is a construction, a composition of elements abstracted from a whole (Schafer, 1983). It is in the interest of putting one foot in front of the other that we ignore in daily living the fact that description, however simple, requires the selection and crystallization of salient details, and their combination and interpretation. Multiple good descriptions of the same phenomenon co-exist. Which is chosen depends upon the deepest purposes that guide our involvement with the phenomenon to be described. In all of life, but with special emphasis in our own field, for "deepest purposes" read "unconscious purposes" or "character style." We can say, then, that which description we choose depends on a great deal more than our conscious orientation. And it is not only the personalities of analyst and patient which are at issue here, but also the part that any particular description of the transference plays in the evolution of the analytic relationship. And finally, the transference itself, as it develops over time, is an influence on its own further understanding.

An Ambivalent Challenge

THERE IS A LINE OF THOUGHT in Dr. Witenberg's paper with which I am in full agreement. This line of thought is one which is opposed to dogmatism and absolutism. It is against the notion that any current theory has a hold on the truth, about either human development and motivation or about correct analytic technique, and also that any theory could, in principle, ever achieve such a degree of certainty. On the contrary, the point of view that Dr. Witenberg espouses is that what we understand, especially in the realm of interpersonal and subjective experience, is always provisional and always relative to certain perspectives that are operating at a given time in the process of exploration. Our understanding is constructed in accord with our world views and theoretical preconceptions as well as our personal, selective sensitivities within the analytic situation.

In addition, Dr. Witenberg points to what I think is an optimal position with respect to theory and its application to any specific clinical situation. He says, for example, "I submit that none of the theories singly or combined is going to solve the dissatisfaction [that is, the dissatisfaction with theory in general]. I find each of them [that is, each theory] useful for certain issues in practice as a way of my having multiple transitional objects. They give me a certain security when I listen to a patient. But I spend an awful lot of time trying to get these theories out of my head so that I can listen to the patient, so that I can generate questions that are more relevant than the existing theories are to this particular person with this particular analyst."

This use of theory strikes me as optimal. The paradox that Dr. Witenberg points to in this and other statements, in which he makes use of and tries to get rid of theoretical preconceptions, is a necessary one.

APPROACHING THE CONCEPT OF idealization from an interpersonal psychoanalytic perspective we might feel that we are in inhospitable waters; this is not a concept that would come easily to the pragmatic, positivist orientation of Harry Stack Sullivan. There is much in Sullivan's work which would, in effect, be counter to this concept of idealization; for example, his emphasis on the illusion of unique individuality and the parataxic and defensive aspects of the individual's view of themself as special. This aspect of his thinking, eventuated in his comforting and egalitarian notion, that "we are all more simply human then otherwise." The thrust of so much of Sullivan's efforts was to help those who felt separate and special by virtue of their sense of inadequacy and parataxic confusion become members of the social community, able to engage in cooperative and collaborative actions. Yet, in our efforts to help the patient move from a parataxic view of the world which, infused with anxiety and primitive fears, to a less anxious, consensual and more objective view of the world, we may miss something of value which is associated with this contemporary notion of idealization.

In psychoanalytic literature, the concept of idealization seems to be used in three different ways, depending upon the individual writer's theoretical orientation. The traditional and ego psychological view is that idealization is a defensive function which is an active or enhanced form of denial. From a Kleinian perspective, idealization is attributed to the early developmental organization of perception in which splitting, the dominant organizational principle, results in a perception of objects as all good or all bad. Idealization of objects, is an aspect of the splitting mechanisms of the paranoid-schizoid position and continues until there is a moderation of aggression and the integration of good and bad objects which occurs in the depressive position. From either the ego psychological position, or the Kleinian position, the analyst's task is the same; to interpret the patient's dissociated or repressed hate and aggression, and to engage in and resolve the intense negative transference.

TWO OF THE MOST IMPORTANT concepts in psychoanalysis are transference and character. Formulating the relationship between the two should enhance our understanding of the patient and produce a more effective approach to treatment. Paradoxically we find these concepts are rarely discussed in relation to each other. In fact they are often treated as if they existed in isolation. Many articles appear every year about transference, while little is written about character. Almost nothing is said about the relationship between the two. At the clinical level we observe that when analysts describe a patient, they usually describe his character. When they describe the treatment, them seem to focus exclusively on the transference with no mention of character.

RECENTLY, THERE HAS BEEN a steady arrival on the scene of a number of works which offer as their aim the qualification of Wilfred Bion's thinking or, to be more exact, about his thinking about thinking. They include Grinberg, Sor, and Tabak de Bianchedi (1975), Meltzer (1978), (1983), Eigen (1981), (1985), Williams (1985), Simon (1986)—and even W. R. Bion and F. Bion (1980).

Boris' (1986) contribution is one which I believe would have pleased Bion. He seems to have captured the quintessence of this elusive man by employing on his palette the pigments of paradox, irony, enigma, complexity, and contradiction, but all with an underlying background of unity—and that unity is Bion's "obsession with Truth." Bion often said that Truth was as necessary to the mind as was food to the gastrointestinal tract. Psychoanalytic Society presidential address (September 17, 1986), From Marginality to Pluralism, sounded a keynote that may also be felt as reverberating in the theme that she and the W.A.W. Psychoanalytic Society Program Chairman John Muñoz have chosen for 1987. I surmise that they believe there is an incentive for and an interest in examing and discussing transcultural factors as they may affect the clinical practice of psychoanalysis. Fully aware of the trust placed in me to start this series, and most appreciative of it, I am approaching the task with some misgivings and some trepidation. What is there to be said about something that should be self-evident? And if, indeed, there is such self-evidence about the subject matter, why does one get the impression that there is either underemphasis, if not blissful ignorance, or overemphasis, if not frantic pursuit in regard to it? But, perhaps, I am getting ahead of myself. Let me start with some clarifications as to the title of this peresentation.

(2) A tendency to view alien groups or cultures in terms of one's own (Random House Dictionary of the English Language, 1966). It is the second definition that applies to my title while, psychoanalytically speaking, the first one may suggest covert motivational aspects for the second. Stephen Mitchell

Stephen Mitchell  

I WANT TO BEGIN BY THANKING Dr. Basch for an excellent, thoughtful paper. As usual, he has given us a rich blend of broad, cross-disciplinary considerations, innovative theoretical constructions, and interesting clinical applications, which places his contribution very much in the spirit that the planners of this conference were striving for.

I find myself in total agreement with Dr. Basch's larger project and many of his basic premises, which I would summarize as follows: 1) Freud's drive theory has for decades been an enormous retardant to the generation of theoretical innovation in our field. 2) The presuppositions of drive theory derive from and are inextricably bound up with now anachronistic principles of 19th century biology and neurophysiology; according to contemporary understanding, the brain is not an apparatus for energetic discharge but an information-processing system for the generation and organization of meanings. 3) Proponents of post-drive theory psychoanalytic models have tended to involve themselves in very destructive acrimony and mutual dismissals, in which each model itself claims to be a complete and sufficient replacement for the enormously comprehensive and intricate drive theory metapsychology. 4) One of the most important tasks in current theory-building is developing a synthesis of the study of interpersonal transactions with the study of intrapsychic processes (the latter separated from the specific content of the intrapsychic suggested by classical drive theory). and 5) In broad strokes, any such theoretical synthesis needs to take as its basic conceptual framework a consideration of more or less unconscious "patterns of expectation" regarding self and others—encoded transactions.

I share this larger vision of Dr. Basch's and thus am in essential agreement with the basic sense of where psychoanalytic theory needs to go. In fact, my impression is that more and more contemporary psychoanalysts from many different backgrounds are in general agreement about where psychoanalytic theory needs to end up, what it needs to encompass.

PRIOR TO PERHAPS TWENTY years ago, most of those psychoanalysts whose dominant theoretical orientation was that of ego psychology and the structural theory held that near-classical psychoanalysis should be used solely in the therapy of neurotics and that individuals whose personality structure lay nearer the psychotic end of the continuum of psychopathological states were best treated by other means. Subsequently, in the United States, psychoanalysis with relatively few parameters (Eissler, 1953) has come to be used more commonly in the treatment of people who are afflicted with at least the less primitive varieties of those conditions that have come to be subsumed under the rubric, borderline personality (Meissner, 1984). It is the thesis of this contribution that a major reason for this change is to be found in the infusion into the thinking of the ego psychologists of portions of the thinking of the so-called British schools of psychoanalysis concerning the development of object relations and a resultant better understanding of transference-countertransference phenomena. PSYCHOANALYSIS HAS PRODUCED FEW gadflies. This is strange in a discipline dedicated to challenging sacred cows. From Freud's debunking man's faith in the rule of reason to every clinician's stock in trade—"Have you looked at it this way?"—analysts have operated as the friendly critics of conventional wisdom. And yet not many writers have had the theoretical breadth, the clinical sensitivity, and the sympathy for analytic goals to raise similar questions about our own fundamental assumptions.

Where would a psychoanalytic gadfly begin? With Freud, certainly, especially with his vision of the discipline as he created it. Freud described the evolution of psychoanalytic theory succinctly in a passage from the New Introductory Lectures describing the development of psychoanalysis from its clinical origins to the elaboration of its theoretical structure. "The path, " he wrote, "led from symptoms to the unconscious, to the life of the instincts, to sexuality …" (1933, p. 57).

The first step on Freud's path, from symptoms—today, of course, we would add all those characteristics that constitute and define the individual personality—to the unconscious, is one that is accepted by all analysts. It has become what Freud might have called a "shibboleth" of modern psychoanalysis. The very concept of a therapeutically beneficial psychoanalytic inquiry, which assumes that one can effect change by broadening the patient's awareness of his experience, would make no sense without an underlying conviction that aspects of experience are kept from consciousness under ordinary circumstances.

The second step—somewhat more controversial—led Freud from the dynamic unconscious to instinct, or drive.

THERE ARE SOME PEOPLE for whom there is no such thing as nothing. In their psychic calculus, zero does not exist. Inside the zero, where there might otherwise be an absence, there is instead a presence of an absence. One patient described the no-thing inside the zero as a breast sticking its tongue out. This was later, when he could afford to be whimsical. Another, looking at the acoustical ceiling tiles, said: "I see a bee (my initial) a Queen bee, actually a stinger; it looks deadly. What is that word? "Anaphylactic" shock. Anaphylactic, such a curious word to be so deadly. "Lactic", "lactose", means milk. "Phil" means love. Yesterday when you reminded me of that word, you said one found one's own antitoxins toxic. … At the end of the session, when I thanked you—it was such a good session—you said the thanks should go to myself—that I owed you nothing. I felt so hurt. So …"

Of noticed clocks on winter afternoons, malignant stars,
Demanding furniture. All unrelated
And with air between. The terror. Is it of Space, of Time?

IN THE INTERPERSONAL WORLD OF THE INFANT Daniel Stern has set himself a monumental task: he not only undertakes to study in minute detail the vagaries of development of a sense of self in the first two years of life, but he also views the infant through the clinical eye of the analyst and finally ends by commenting on the relevance of his findings to clinical work. Stern has succeeded in outlining his findings and subsequent inferences extremely clearly; in addition he has challenged some well established analytic notions of development, and has suggested a bridge between development as observed and later pathology. With it all he has remained clear about his own interpersonal theoretical thrust while at the same time being respectful of the theoretical contributions of others.

Central to the book as a whole is Stern's respect for the infant, its psyche and its interpersonal world, a respect not always found among analytic theoreticians who have often viewed the infant "through a glass darkly", that is from an adultomorphic distance. This distant, adult perspective ascribes all manner of psychic life to the infant, usually in clinical and ultimately in pathologic terms. Given that few analysts have chosen to spend time in the nursery, their theories are by necessity based on inferences from their work with adult patients. Those who have used infant observation, Mahler, Bowlby and others, have either not had access to the kind of technology that lends itself to finely tuned observations and to actual experimentation, or they too have had a predetermined view of the infant. More often than not the infant has been described as either being at the mercy of drives, or as being symbiotically merged and needing help to move in the direction of separation and individuation. In either case the interpersonal world is mainly seen as instrumental in encouraging the infant to develop from an undifferentiated state towards becoming a functioning person. Stern does not reject the notion that the interpersonal environment has this function, but he challenges the assumption that the infant is undifferentiated, unable to assess reality or totally helpless in his interaction with the care-taking adult.

WHO WOULD ARGUE WITH the proposition that in the ideal analysis positive as well as negative feelings toward the analyst should eventually become the subject of thorough, evenhanded investigation. It

491

is my impression, however, that recent theorizing, particularly emphasis on the working alliance, the real relationship, and the empathic response, has moved us further and further away from a theory of technique which encourages actively questioning the positive transference. I define positive transference as any positive feelings directed toward the analyst. This definition underscores the premise that the transference and "non-transference" elements of such positive feelings are deeply intertwined and can never be fully separated.

I am suggesting that theoretical considerations as well as institutional and countertransference forces work to deflect us from carefully scrutinizing the varied elements of the positive transference. In addition, I believe a potential transference-countertransference problem may occur when the patient's positive view of the analyst coincides with the analyst's perception of himself or herself.

Freud, in his papers on technique (1912), (1913), (1914), held that transference need only be analyzed when it functions as a resistance. These transference resistances include both negative reactions and unconscious erotic feelings. The unobjectionable part of the positive transference, the "friendly or affectionate feelings which are admissable to consciousness, " were seen as important in strengthening the attachment to the analyst and in helping the patient overcome his or her resistance to change. Freud (1913) also stressed the significance of the "effective transference, " that is the trusting, working relationship that must be established prior to the analyst's making interpretations.

Freud (1915) differentiated these aspects of the positive transference from the erotic positive transference, which he saw not only as a resistance but, as in the case of intractable transference love, as a factor that could undermine and even destroy the analysis. In 1937, he acknowledged that the unobjectionable transference contained elements of unconscious conflict.

I HAVE BEEN FOLLOWING DANIEL STERN'S research for many years with interest and admiration. Even now, though I have serious reservations concerning his interpretations of that research, I still agree with Gifford's (1986) review of Stern's first book, The First Relationship(1977), "This book not only holds its own in the great descriptive tradition of Spitz, Escalona, Wolff, and other gifted observers of the newborn, but its warm, contagious style conveys some of the exhilaration—that delight in seeing familiar phenomena in a new way—we encountered on first reading Spitz's early papers" (p. 226).

Gifford goes on to observe that Stern was dealing lightly with the contrast between his observations and traditional psychoanalytic views of infancy, "even treating Freud's original intuitions with sympathy and respect," and allowing for reconciliations between certain old views of infancy and certain new ones (p. 226).

In contrast, Stern's latest volume, The Interpersonal World of the Infant(1985), leaves very little room for negotiation between the old and the new. Now Stern has it that his studies of infant development will revolutionize psychoanalytic theory and clinical practice. And, judging from the endorsements on the book jacket, very few psychoanalysts, impressed as they are with anyone who is engaged in "hard" research, are willing to point out the flaws in Stern's interpretation of his data or his questionable grasp of traditional psychoanalytic theory.

The liveliness of Stern's personality and manner of presentation, welcome as they might be in a general atmosphere of stifling orthodoxy, should not be confused with the long-range relevance of his ideas. It is one thing to appreciate the value of Stern's research data and his inventive research methodology and quite another to accept Stern's unverified hypotheses on the emergence of the self as a replacement for the psychoanalytic model of the infant mind.

Paul Roazen  

THE SUBJECT OF PSYCHOANALYTIC BIOGRAPHY ought to sound alarm-bells in the minds of fair-minded observers. So much tendentions stuff has appeared throughout this century, under the banner of "applying" either Freud's ideas or the concepts of some of his disciples, that neutral witnesses with a concern for impartial history are entitled to be wary of what looks like zealots prosletizing in behalf of their beliefs. But if we start by asking the question of whether psychoanalytic biography still exists, and if so whether it deserves to continue or thrive, I am hoping that the topic will hold the attention even of those most likely to scoff.

Curiously enough Freud's most ardent so-called defenders are apt not to want to think on his own biographical studies. It is one of the few subjects on which orthodox analysts might be relieved not to have to begin with Freud. Yet I think that his studies of Leonardo and also Moses, and even his book with William C. Bullitt on Woodrow Wilson, need not cause nearly as much embarrassment as has been thought; although Freud's few comments on biography-writing occasionally get quoted, his own biographical efforts rarely appear in the professional literature (Roazen, 1968). If one approaches Freud not in search of infallibility, but as a model of originality and daring, then his biographies begin to look as considerable as anything else he did. The Leonardo book, for example, has many things wrong with it that any beginning student ought now to be able to point out. But it remains a remarkable work of art that will nonetheless endure in intellectual history. Almost half a century later Erik H. Erikson's Young Man Luther had its own flaws, yet we would be lucky to have more such creative achievements (Roazen, 1976a).

"… the souls of men are the gift from language to mankind." Alfred North Whitehead (1938, p.41)

THE GESTALT PSYCHOLOGIST WOLFGANG KOHLER once surmised that if a fish were to become a scientist, this scientist-fish's last discovery would be water, given it's ubiquitous and therefore all too familiar presence. In psychoanalytic theory, the same might be said of language. While Freud's discovery of the repression of words was the virtual starting point of psychoanalytic inquiry, the word is taken (by Freud and his "mainline" followers) as a manifestation of the self's functioning, rather than as an actual feature of that functioning. Among interpersonal analysts, while Sullivan placed great emphasis upon the consensual validation language brings to our development, he and his followers have had little to say about the role language plays as a structural feature of the self. That is, language has been appreciated as a medium of communication; it has been neglected as a structure that, as proposed some time ago by Mead (1934), transforms the individual into a social, self conscious being.

Recently, Levenson (1983) has responded to this neglect by proposing "semiotic competence" as a principal goal of psychoanalytic work—the capacity to effectively relate what is said to what is done. In this essay, I follow Levenson's lead, in terms of an assumption concerning the work, that the individual must develop some awareness of him or her self as a creator of meaning; and of language as our principal medium for the realization of meaning. An understanding of how language functions in relation to the self is therefore seen as critical to our understanding of psychoanalytic practice.

THIS BOOK,1 SOLIDLY BASED ON the careful research of Daniel Stern and associates, provides the basis for developmental theory that almost defies controversy. The approach differs from most attempts to document psychological and psychoanalytic theory in that it does not start out with adultamorphic concepts and then seek evidence to support them. It is much closer to the traditional experimental approach with null-hypotheses. There are truly no preconceived notions about child behavior that are being tested but instead there is a careful examination of research and experimentation with infants, which Stern then uses to construct theoretical concepts.

The volume clearly will be the book of the decade in its influence on psychoanalytic theory. It is of sufficient magnitude and importance that no contemporary theorist can ignore it.

Edgar Levenson  

MY ESTEEMED UNCLE, SAM LEVENSON (whom some of you older folks may remember as a TV folk humorist and author), used to say about his family that there were seven brothers and one sister and not one looked the slightest bit like any other—but they all looked like Papa! Much the same situation exists in psychoanalysis. No matter how unrelated our metaphysical and clinical positions appear to be; there is, nevertheless, an uneasy persistent family resemblance. We are all psychoanalysts.

The inference is that we must be doing something in common, tapping into some cognitive process in the patient. In Khan's felicitous phrase, we are all the servants of the patient's process (Khan, 1969). The problem is that we have great difficulty saying what it is we do when we do what we do. This is really not so unique to our field. The gap between what we can do and what we can say about it is universal.
